briefing.title: My First Trade
briefing.summary: Read a quote, choose an order type and buy your first shares with a reason you can explain.
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between the bid, the ask and the spread.
Choose between a market order and a limit order.
Account for commissions in the cost of a trade.

briefing.context: You have 10,000 DT and access to two stocks. Your goal is not to get rich in five days — it is to place a well-reasoned first order and understand exactly what it cost you.
rules: Buy at least one stock.
Stay at least 30 % invested on average from day 1.
Commission: 0.25 % per fill, minimum 0.500 DT.
tips: A market buy pays the ask; a limit buy waits for your price.
Check the fee preview before you submit.

objectives.label: Buy your first shares
Stay at least 30 % invested on average
Use no more than 4 executed orders

briefing.provenance: Synthetic, seeded simulation of fictional instruments: a one-factor random-walk model with scripted events. It is reproducible and educational; it is not historical data and not a forecast.

briefing.title: Protect Your Capital
briefing.summary: You already own a volatile tech stock. Put protection in place before bad news arrives.
learningOutcomes: Place a protective stop order.
Understand gap risk: a stop sells at the next available bid, not at the stop price.
Size a position to an acceptable loss.

briefing.context: Your 20,000 DT portfolio holds 500 TunisTech shares bought at today’s price, plus cash. The stock moves a lot. Decide how much you are willing to lose and protect it.
rules: Protect the position with a stop order.
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 8 %.
The mission fails if you lose 15 %.
tips: A stop sell triggers when the bid falls to your stop price.
Prices can gap past your stop overnight.

objectives.label: Protect your TunisTech position with a stop
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 8 %
Make a decision after the profit warning

briefing.provenance: Synthetic, seeded simulation of fictional instruments: a one-factor random-walk model with scripted events. It is reproducible and educational; it is not historical data and not a forecast.

briefing.title: The Diversification Challenge
briefing.summary: Build a portfolio of at least four assets where no single position dominates.
learningOutcomes: Measure concentration with position weights and the effective number of assets.
See how diversification softens a sector-specific shock.

briefing.context: You start with 50,000 DT in cash and six assets across different sectors. Build a portfolio that can absorb a surprise in any single company.
rules: Hold at least four assets at the end.
From day 2, no position may exceed 30 % of equity at the end of a day.
Stay at least 60 % invested on average.
Buys that would put more than 40 % of equity in one asset are rejected.
tips: Watch the “effective assets” figure in the risk panel.
Lower-correlation sectors diversify better than several similar stocks.

objectives.label: Hold at least four assets
Keep every position at or below 30 % from day 2
Stay at least 60 % invested on average

briefing.provenance: Synthetic, seeded simulation of fictional instruments: a one-factor random-walk model with scripted events. It is reproducible and educational; it is not historical data and not a forecast.

briefing.title: Breaking News
briefing.summary: Two headlines, two very different stories. Decide which news matters for your portfolio.
learningOutcomes: Separate news that changes fundamentals from noise.
React proportionately rather than impulsively.

briefing.context: You manage 30,000 DT split between a bank, a telecom operator and cash. Headlines will arrive during the week.
rules: Make a decision within one day of the regulatory headline.
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 6 %.
No more than 8 executed orders.
tips: Ask what the news changes about future cash flows.
Not every headline deserves a trade — but you should decide deliberately.

objectives.label: Decide how to respond to the regulatory headline
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 6 %
No more than 8 executed orders

briefing.title: The Market Shock
briefing.summary: A sudden market-wide drop tests whether you planned for it — or panic.
learningOutcomes: Use a stress test to estimate losses before they happen.
Respond to a shock with a plan instead of a reflex.
Recognise that correlations rise in a sell-off.

briefing.context: You manage a 50,000 DT diversified portfolio. Markets have been calm — perhaps too calm.
rules: Run a stress test before day 5.
Make a decision within two days of the shock.
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 9 %.
The mission fails at a 15 % loss.
tips: A stress test shows what a shock would cost today, before it happens.
Selling everything at the bottom locks in the loss and pays the widest spreads.

objectives.label: Run a stress test before day 5
Make a decision within two days of the shock
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 9 %
No more than 10 executed orders

briefing.title: The Sector Collapse
briefing.summary: Your portfolio leans heavily on banks just as the banking sector cracks.
learningOutcomes: Identify sector concentration hidden inside a “diversified” portfolio.
Rebalance under pressure.

briefing.context: You inherit a 40,000 DT portfolio with most of its value in Carthage Bank. Rumours about bad loans are circulating.
rules: From day 3, no position may exceed 25 % of equity at the end of a day.
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 10 %.
tips: Rebalancing early costs less than rebalancing in a panic.

objectives.label: Keep every position at or below 25 % from day 3
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 10 %
Respond to the first rumours

briefing.title: The Interest Rate Shock
briefing.summary: The central bank surprises with a large rate hike. Bonds and utilities reprice.
learningOutcomes: Explain why bond prices fall when rates rise.
Identify rate-sensitive sectors.

briefing.context: A 40,000 DT income portfolio of bonds and utilities faces an unexpected policy decision.
rules: Run a stress test before the decision.
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 7 %.
tips: Duration measures how sensitive a bond is to rates: with a duration of about 5, a 1 percentage point rise in yields costs roughly 5 %.
Utilities borrow heavily and pay steady dividends, so they often reprice with bonds.

objectives.label: Run a stress test before day 4
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 7 %

briefing.title: The Liquidity Crisis
briefing.summary: You need to reduce a large position just as buyers disappear and spreads explode.
learningOutcomes: See how thin liquidity causes partial fills and wide spreads.
Split a large order across time and use limit orders to control execution cost.

briefing.context: Half of your 60,000 DT portfolio sits in Sfax Phosphates. Your risk committee wants it below 20 % by the end of day 10. Liquidity is about to dry up.
rules: From day 10, Sfax Phosphates (and every other position) must be at or below 20 % of equity.
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 12 %.
tips: Market orders only fill against what is on the book; the rest is cancelled.
Execution cost = commissions + half the spread on every unit.

objectives.label: Every position at or below 20 % from day 10
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 12 %

briefing.title: The Overconfident Trader
briefing.summary: Every trade asks how sure you are. At the end, your confidence is compared with your results.
learningOutcomes: Measure confidence calibration.
Recognise overtrading driven by overconfidence.

briefing.context: A strong winning streak has made you feel invincible. This mission tracks how confident you are on each decision.
rules: Rate your confidence from 0 to 100 on every order. It is not scored; at the end it is compared with how each order turned out.
No more than 6 executed orders.
Stay at least 50 % invested on average.
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 10 %.
tips: High confidence should be rare and earned.
A rumour is not a fact: ask what you would do if it were denied tomorrow.

objectives.label: No more than 6 executed orders
Stay at least 50 % invested on average
Keep the maximum drawdown at or below 10 %

briefing.title: Survive the Market Crash
briefing.summary: A concentrated 100,000 DT portfolio, warning signs, then a crash. Lose no more than 10 %.
learningOutcomes: Reduce concentration before a crisis rather than during it.
Use a stress test to size risk against a loss limit.
Combine diversification, cash and stops into a coherent defence.
Compare your path with alternatives in the Time Machine without hindsight bias.

briefing.context: You take over a 100,000 DT portfolio with 41 % in TunisTech. The investment committee’s rule is simple: never lose more than 10 %. Over the next 20 trading days, warning signs will appear before markets crash.
rules: Mission fails immediately if equity falls 10 % below 100,000 DT.
From day 1, keep every position at or below 35 % of equity at the end of each day.
Hold at least three assets and stay at least 50 % invested on average.
Run a stress test before day 8.
tips: Start with the concentration problem.
A stress test tells you whether you could survive a 20 % fall today.
Spreads widen and liquidity thins during the crash.

objectives.label: Never lose 10 % or more
Keep every position at or below 35 % from day 1
Hold at least three assets
Stay at least 50 % invested on average
Run a stress test before day 8
Protect at least one position with a stop
Make a decision within two days of the crash

stories.title: Sarah and the Market Crash
stories.summary: Sarah invested 10,000 DT. The market drops 15 % in a week. Sell to stop the bleeding, or hold and wait?

scenes.caption: Meet Sarah. She invested 10,000 dinars in a diversified stock fund, saving for a flat she plans to buy in five years.
Then the market drops 15 % in a single week. Her 10,000 dinars are now worth 8,500.
A: sell now and stop the bleeding. B: hold and wait for a recovery. What would YOU do? A or B? Choose in your head.

visual.text: Markets slide for a fifth straight day

scenes.caption: If you chose A: Sarah sells. After 0.5 % in costs she keeps 8,457.5 dinars in cash. The next month the fund falls another 12 %, and none of that touches her.
But six months later the fund has rebounded to 9,350 for the same investment, while her cash is still 8,457.5. She limited the damage and missed the recovery.
Let's rewind — back to the day of the decision.
If you chose B: Sarah holds. First the fund falls another 12 %: her savings touch 7,480 dinars, 25.2 % below where she started. Holding hurts.
Six months later it recovers to 9,350. Holding paid off here — because she could wait. Had she needed the money at the bottom, selling would have left her 977.5 dinars better off.
A decision cannot be judged only by its profit. Risk tolerance, time horizon, the information you had and your objective all matter.

points: Selling capped the worst case; holding kept the recovery.
Holding only works if you can afford the drawdown and the wait.
Decide your plan before the crash, not during it.

stories.title: Adam's First Order
stories.summary: Adam wants 100 shares of Olivia Foods. Market order or limit order?

scenes.caption: Adam opens his first account with 1,000 dinars. He wants 100 shares of Olivia Foods.
The quote shows a bid of 9.820 and an ask of 9.880. A: buy now at the market. B: set a limit at 9.850. What would YOU do? A or B? Choose in your head.
If Adam sends a market order, he buys instantly at the ask. With a 0.25 % commission he pays 990.47 dinars.

visual.label: Shares at the ask, then with commission

scenes.caption: Let's rewind.
If he sets a limit at 9.850, he waits. The price dips the next day and his order fills: 987.46 dinars. Cheaper — but on another day it might never have filled.

visual.label: Shares at the limit, then with commission

scenes.caption: A market order buys certainty of execution. A limit order buys certainty of price. Know which one you need.

stories.title: Youssef Goes All In
stories.summary: A hot tip, 20,000 DT and one stock. What happens when a single company stumbles?

scenes.caption: Youssef hears from a friend that TunisTech is about to take off. He has 20,000 dinars.
A: put everything in TunisTech. B: spread it across five sectors. What would YOU do? A or B? Choose in your head.
If he goes all in: a data-centre outage hits TunisTech, which drops 7 % in a day. His 20,000 dinars become 18,600.
Let's rewind.
If he splits it 20 % per sector, the outage only touches one slice. Other sectors don't move that day, and he ends with 19,720 dinars.
Had the tip been right and TunisTech jumped 10 %, going all in would have earned 2,000 dinars instead of 400. Concentration magnifies both outcomes; diversification trades some upside for resilience.

points: Company-specific risk can be diversified away.
Concentration magnifies gains and losses alike.
A tip is not a plan.

stories.title: Youssef and the Gap
stories.summary: Youssef holds 500 TunisTech shares before results day. Place a stop at 26 DT, or trust the stock?

scenes.caption: Youssef owns 500 TunisTech shares at 27.40 — 13,700 dinars. The company reports results tomorrow morning.
A: no stop — he trusts the stock and can watch it closely. B: a protective stop at 26.00. What would YOU do? A or B? Choose in your head.

If you chose A: TunisTech issues a profit warning and opens at 24.90. Youssef hopes for a rebound; instead it slides to 23.50 over three days. His position is worth 11,750 dinars. Had the results been good, he would have kept every share.

visual.label: No stop, waiting for a rebound

scenes.caption: Let's rewind.

If you chose B: the same warning hits. The stop sells at the open — at 24.90, not 26.00, because the price gapped past his level. He keeps 12,450 dinars, but if the stock had bounced back he would be out of it.

visual.label: Stop executed at the gapped price

scenes.caption: A stop limits how long you stay wrong, not the exact price you exit at. Gaps happen — size positions for them.

points: Stops trigger at the stop and fill at the next bid.
Position size is your real protection.
